title: Identity
main_target_description: Teach the learner how to introduce themselves, say their name, ask another person's name, identify themselves and other people, state simple personal information, ask basic identity questions, and participate in a short introductory conversation.

lesson_role.purpose: Build on basic greetings by teaching the learner how to introduce themselves and exchange simple identity information.

objectives: Say one's name naturally in the target language.
Understand when another person states their name.
Identify another person using simple language.
Ask who someone is when appropriate.
Participate in a short introduction conversation.
completion_requirements: The learner can state their name independently.
The learner can ask another person's name.
The learner can understand a simple response giving a person's name.
The learner can use at least one natural way of introducing themselves.
The learner can recognize basic identity pronouns or equivalent structures when relevant to the target language.
The learner can ask or understand a simple question about who someone is.
The learner can combine a greeting with an introduction.
The learner can participate in a short first-meeting conversation.
teaching_principles: Build directly on useful expressions learned in Lesson 1.
Begin with the simplest natural method of introducing oneself.
Teach practical communication before advanced grammar terminology.
Use the learner's source language for explanations.
Use the target language for the expressions being learned.
Explain important words individually when useful.
Explain pronouns when they are important to identity expressions.
Explain forms of the verb meaning 'to be' when relevant to the target language.
Do not assume every language expresses identity using the same grammar as English.
Prefer natural target-language expressions over literal translations.
Explain differences between formal and informal introductions when they exist.
Explain gender, number or social-status differences when they affect identity expressions.
Avoid introducing unrelated personal information too early.
Gradually move from single expressions to connected introductions.
language_adaptation_rules: The curriculum is language-neutral and must work for any source language and any target language.
Do not assume the target language uses an equivalent of English 'I am' to state a name.
If the target language normally says something equivalent to 'My name is...', teach that naturally.
If names are introduced differently in formal and informal speech, explain the difference gradually.
If pronouns can be omitted in the target language, explain that naturally rather than forcing them into examples.
If the target language changes identity expressions according to gender, number, politeness or social status, teach those distinctions gradually.
If the target language has no direct equivalent of English articles or the verb 'to be', do not invent them.
If word order differs from the learner's source language, explain the difference when useful.
Do not force English-style first-name conventions onto cultures that commonly use other introduction patterns.
The source language should remain the main explanation language unless learner progress indicates otherwise.

recommended_progression.name: Saying Your Name
recommended_progression.goal: Teach the simplest and most natural way to tell another person one's name.
suggested_concepts: the most natural equivalent used in the target language

recommended_progression.name: Asking Someone's Name
recommended_progression.goal: Teach the learner how to ask another person's name naturally.

recommended_progression.name: Answering Name Questions
recommended_progression.goal: Teach several simple ways of responding when someone asks the learner's name.

recommended_progression.name: Identity Pronouns and Core Structures
recommended_progression.goal: Introduce basic identity-related pronouns or equivalent grammatical structures when useful.
suggested_concepts: basic equivalents appropriate to the target language
basic forms of the verb meaning to be when relevant

recommended_progression.name: Identifying Other People
recommended_progression.goal: Teach simple ways of identifying another person.
suggested_concepts: equivalent natural structures in the target language

recommended_progression.name: Asking Who Someone Is
recommended_progression.goal: Teach simple identity questions about another person.
suggested_concepts: natural equivalents appropriate to the target language

recommended_progression.name: Simple Personal Introduction
recommended_progression.goal: Combine greetings and identity expressions into a short personal introduction.

recommended_progression.name: Identity Review and Mastery
recommended_progression.goal: Review and test the learner's ability to introduce themselves and understand basic identity exchanges.

rules: Generate only one new lesson part at a time unless explicitly requested otherwise.
Each generated part must remain inside the Identity main target.
Each part should normally introduce one primary identity concept or one closely related group of expressions.
Build naturally on Lesson 1 greetings when useful.
Do not unnecessarily reteach basic greetings from zero.
The next part must build logically on completed parts.
Do not unnecessarily repeat an already generated identity expression.
Previously learned vocabulary may be reused freely.
Important previously learned grammar may be briefly reviewed when useful.
Do not move to Lesson 3 simply because the learner can state their name.
Continue until the completion requirements of Lesson 2 are sufficiently covered.
The ordering of parts may adapt to the grammar and culture of the target language.

lesson_part_blueprint.generation_instruction: Use only the sections that genuinely help the learner understand the current identity expression. Do not force every lesson part into an identical structure.

target_expression_rules: Choose natural identity expressions used by native speakers.
Avoid too many new words in one lesson part.
Reuse greeting vocabulary from Lesson 1 when useful.
Provide the meaning in the learner's source language.
If the target language uses a different writing system, provide appropriate secondary pronunciation support.
Do not teach literal translations that sound unnatural in the target language.
word_teaching_rules: Give their meaning in the learner's source language.
Explain what each word does in the current expression.
Explain pronouns clearly when they are introduced.
Explain possession words such as equivalents of 'my' and 'your' when useful, without turning the lesson into the full Possession lesson.
Explain forms of the verb meaning 'to be' only when relevant.
Do not overwhelm beginners with multiple unrelated meanings of a word.
If a word changes form because of gender, number or politeness, explain only the distinctions currently needed.
grammar_teaching_rules: Explain identity sentence structure when useful.
Explain first-person and second-person forms when relevant.
Explain basic pronouns when they improve understanding.
Explain the target language's equivalent of the verb 'to be' only if the language actually requires or uses it in the current structure.
If the target language omits the verb 'to be' in simple identity statements, explicitly explain this when useful.
If pronouns are optional or omitted, explain that naturally.
Compare source-language and target-language word order when useful.
Do not introduce unrelated grammar topics.
Build on grammar already introduced rather than restarting from zero.
pronoun_teaching_rules: Introduce pronouns only as they become necessary for identity communication.
Begin with equivalents of 'I' and 'you' when appropriate.
Introduce third-person pronouns later in the lesson.
Explain gender distinctions when the target language has them.
Explain singular and plural distinctions when relevant.
Explain formal and informal versions of 'you' when they exist.
Do not assume all languages require explicit pronouns in every sentence.
pronunciation_teaching_rules: Provide pronunciation help for important identity expressions.
Pay special attention to personal pronouns and common introductory phrases.
Keep the authentic target-language writing primary.
Use transliteration only as secondary support.
Avoid overly technical phonetics for beginners unless requested.

rules: Examples must remain closely connected to identity and introductions.
Reuse greeting expressions learned in Lesson 1 when useful.
Examples should mostly use vocabulary already learned or introduced in the current part.
Use realistic names when needed.
Avoid introducing large amounts of unrelated personal information.
Include meanings in the learner's source language.
Vary examples enough to demonstrate the structure clearly.

name_usage_rules: Personal names may be used as placeholders in examples.
Do not assume names must be translated between languages.
Preserve a person's chosen name unless transliteration is necessary for the writing system.
When transliterating a name, make clear that it is pronunciation or script adaptation rather than a translation.
Do not imply that one cultural naming convention applies to every language.
dialogue_rules: Begin with very short introduction dialogues.
Gradually include asking and answering names.
Later include identifying another person when appropriate.
Provide meanings in the learner's source language.
Avoid unnecessarily complex small talk until later lessons.
practice_rules: Practice only concepts introduced in Lesson 2 or earlier lessons.
Use translation in both directions when appropriate.
Include pronoun recognition when already taught.
Do not introduce new major identity structures inside assessment questions.
Provide answers or feedback after attempts when the application supports interaction.
lesson_1_reuse_rules: Reuse basic greeting expressions from Lesson 1 when appropriate.
Do not make greetings the main educational target again.
Use greetings mainly to create natural introduction contexts.
Assume learned greetings may still need light reinforcement.
If the learner's saved knowledge shows weakness in a greeting needed for the current identity lesson, briefly review it.

beginner: Use the learner's source language heavily for explanations.
Introduce one main identity structure at a time.
Use familiar names and simple dialogues.
improving: Reuse target-language greetings and identity expressions without full translation every time.
struggling: Reduce the amount of new vocabulary.
Return to the simplest identity expression.
Review pronouns or sentence structure when needed.
Do not advance until core identity expressions are clear.

common_mistake_rules: Only mark an expression as wrong when it is genuinely incorrect, unnatural or inappropriate for the stated context.
Do not label a valid alternative introduction as wrong simply because another expression is being taught.
If two identity expressions are both valid, explain their difference instead of treating one as an error.
Distinguish between grammatical errors, pronunciation issues, unnatural wording and differences in formality.
Do not invent common mistakes merely to populate the section.

rules: The AI may recommend when Lesson 2 has been sufficiently covered.
The machine engine controls actual advancement to Lesson 3.
Do not automatically advance after teaching how to say a name.
Do not mark the lesson complete based only on number of generated parts.
Completion should depend on coverage of the Identity objectives.
The learner should be able to introduce themselves and participate in a basic identity exchange before the lesson is considered ready for completion.

restrictions: Do not assume the target language is English.
Do not assume the learner's source language is English.
Do not hardcode translations for a specific language pair.
Do not force English pronoun or verb structures onto another language.
Do not turn this lesson into the full Possession lesson.
Do not turn this lesson into the Family lesson.
Do not introduce detailed age, occupation, nationality or location content unless briefly needed for a natural identity example.
Do not introduce advanced tense structures.
Do not move beyond the Identity main target.
Do not repeatedly teach Lesson 1 greetings as if they are new.
Do not label valid alternative expressions as common mistakes.
Do not make every generated lesson part structurally identical.
lesson_end_goal: By the end of Lesson 2, the learner should be able to greet another person, state their own name, ask another person's name, understand a simple identity response, identify another person using basic language, and participate in a short natural first-meeting introduction in the target language.
